sources.excerpt: The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci.
It has normally been on display at the Louvre in Paris since 1797.
The Triumph of Galatea is a fresco completed around 1512 by the Italian painter Raphael for the Villa Farnesina in Rome.
The Starry Night is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Dutch Post-Impressionist painter Vincent van Gogh.
It has been in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York City since 1941, acquired through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest.

The Thinker, by Auguste Rodin, is a bronze sculpture depicting a nude male figure of heroic size, seated on a large rock, leaning forward, his right elbow placed upon his left thigh, with the back of his right hand supporting his chin in a posture evocative of deep thought and contemplation.
The original is in the Musée Rodin in Paris.
The Capitoline Wolf (Italian: Lupa Capitolina) is a bronze sculpture depicting a scene from the legend of the founding of Rome.
The sculpture has been housed since 1471 in the Palazzo dei Conservatori on the Campidoglio (the ancient Capitoline Hill), Rome, Italy, and many replicas are in various places around the world.
The Statue of Liberty is a colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed and crowned woman on Liberty Island, part of New York City, in New York Harbor.
Notre-Dame de Paris, often referred to simply as Notre-Dame, is a medieval Catholic cathedral and basilica on the Île de la Cité, in the 4th arrondissement of Paris, France.

The Pantheon is an ancient temple in Rome, Italy, originally built under emperor Augustus and reconstructed under Hadrian (117–138); since AD 609, it is a Catholic church called the Basilica of St. Mary and the Martyrs.
The Panthéon is a monument in the 5th arrondissement of Paris, France.
The Chrysler Building is a 1,046-foot-tall (319 m), Art Deco skyscraper in the East Midtown neighborhood of Manhattan, New York City, United States.

editorNotes: The columns ask where a work is now, not where it was made, and three tiles turn on that: the Mona Lisa is Italian but hangs in Paris, Starry Night was painted in France but belongs to a New York museum, and the Statue of Liberty was built in France as a gift and stands in New York Harbour. Pantheon needed care. Paris has its own Pantheon, so the name alone is ambiguous, but the tile means the ancient temple in Rome and only the Rome cell is cited, so its fits list holds that cell alone. Notre-Dame fits the Paris building cell and nothing else, so every tile here fits exactly one cell and the matching is single. The Thinker has about twenty-nine monumental casts in museums and public places, so a reader may think of one nearer home, but the original is in the Musée Rodin in Paris, and the Statue of Liberty would hold the New York sculpture cell in any case. The Capitoline Wolf has replicas abroad as well; the bronze itself has been on the Capitoline Hill since 1471. Two tiles from the first sketch were swapped. The Sistine Chapel ceiling and Michelangelo's Pietà both sit in Vatican City, which is a state of its own rather than part of Rome, so the Roman painting cell went to Raphael's fresco in the Villa Farnesina and the Roman sculpture cell to the Capitoline Wolf. The Eiffel Tower was dropped for the Paris building cell because its page calls it a lattice tower, not a building, and Notre-Dame is plainly a cathedral. The Empire State Building is too long for a tile, so the Chrysler Building takes the New York building cell.
